short: Fourteen years of Danube warfare consumed the reign Marcus Aurelius spent writing the Meditations.
full:
From 166 CE, Germanic Marcomanni and Quadi and Sarmatian Iazyges broke across the Danube frontier in numbers Rome had not faced there before, at one point pushing raiders as far as Aquileia in northern Italy. Marcus Aurelius, ruling jointly with Lucius Verus and then alone after 169, spent most of his remaining reign commanding campaigns from forward bases at Carnuntum and Sirmium rather than from Rome, famously composing his private philosophical notebook, the Meditations, on campaign.

A revolt by the general Avidius Cassius in 175 forced a temporary truce, but fighting resumed and continued until Marcus's death at Vindobona in 180. His son and successor Commodus made peace on terms less punitive than his father intended, withdrawing rather than annexing new territory across the Danube. The wars exposed how thinly stretched the empire's northern frontier had become and foreshadowed the pressures that would recur through the third century.
